analysis.one_liner: Imposes legal duties on online companies to secure, limit use of, and not sell users' personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2023 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Data Care Act would have required online companies — from social media platforms to websites and apps — to act as careful stewards of the personal data they collect about users. Companies would have to secure data against hackers, tell users when sensitive data is breached, avoid using data in ways that foreseeably harm users, and refuse to sell or share data unless the recipient takes on the same responsibilities. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce these duties. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use the internet: anyone whose Social Security number, health records, precise location, biometrics, or private messages are collected online. The bill would have given them enforceable rights — security, prompt breach notice, protection against exploitative uses, and the ability to hold companies accountable through the FTC and their state attorney general — and barred companies from writing those protections out of their contracts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes three enforceable duties on online service providers: reasonably secure people's data, don't use it in ways that foreseeably harm users, and don't pass it on to anyone else unless that party accepts the same duties.

It covers sensitive data specifically — Social Security numbers, health information, precise location, biometrics, financial account numbers, and private messages — and requires providers to promptly tell users if that data is breached.

It lets the FTC and state attorneys general sue violators, with civil penalties scaled to the number of days of violation or the number of users harmed, and it bars companies from writing the protections out of their user agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Online service providers — social media platforms, websites, apps, and the data-broker and digital-advertising businesses built on selling user information. They would owe a legal duty of care toward user data, face lawsuits and per-day or per-user penalties for violations, and could no longer freely share or sell data to partners who don't accept the same duties.

drawbacks.text: The duties are framed in general terms — 'reasonably secure,' 'reasonably foreseeable and material harm,' 'unexpected and highly offensive' — leaving their exact scope to FTC regulation and future litigation, which would take years to settle.
Compliance costs fall on companies of all sizes; the FTC may consider a provider's size when writing exemptions, but small websites and services bear auditing and contract obligations from day one.

Enforcement runs through the FTC and state attorneys general rather than private lawsuits by individuals, so affected users depend on those officials to act; the bill also lets the FTC block a state action while its own case is pending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful: a clear, enforceable duty of care over the personal data companies collect, with penalties scaled to how many people were harmed and how long a violation lasted, and no fine print to waive it. The main costs fall on companies, and honest supporters should acknowledge real tradeoffs: compliance and audit costs would be heaviest for small providers, the FTC's power to write exemptions gives regulated industries a channel to seek carve-outs, and enforcement depends on regulators and state attorneys general pursuing cases rather than on individuals suing on their own. On balance the bill aimed to shift a real risk — identity theft, sensitive-data exposure, exploitative data use — from individuals to the companies that profit from the data. It never got the chance, because it died in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the session ended.

narrative.text: The bill's only actions were its introduction on March 9, 2023 and its referral to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Congress.gov records the bill's last action as its referral to committee, with the 118th Congress having ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect, sell, and use Americans' personal data, which keep operating under the current patchwork of rules without a general duty of care — and the committee leadership that avoided a contested privacy fight. Ordinary users got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality for online service providers.

for.name: 19 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 17 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 4 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Cortez Masto, Merkley, Warren, Klobuchar, Sanders, Markey, Booker, Durbin, King, and others.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Large technology and digital advertising companies
against.what_they_did: Have broadly opposed comprehensive federal privacy legislation that would impose enforceable duties on how they collect, use, and sell personal data.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past a Democratic-led committee referral.

industries.industry: Online platforms and large technology companies
industries.note: They would owe a legal duty of care over user data and could be sued by the FTC and state attorneys general, with penalties that scale with the number of users harmed — costs and legal exposure they do not face today.
The confidentiality duty restricts selling or sharing user data unless the recipient accepts the same duties, which constrains the market for reselling personal information.

They collect personal data too and would bear compliance costs, though the FTC may write exemptions based on a provider's size, the complexity of its offerings, and the sensitivity of the data it handles.
